sources.news_title: Technical glitch at JPMorgan Chase impacts online banking at major US banks: What we know so far
JPMorgan bug causes transaction problems at US banks
sources.text:
Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
However, Chase said that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and that it was working to bring banking services back online by the end of the day on Monday.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system – it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank.
The disruption comes days after two major outages affected other parts of the US economy: A major outage by Microsoft happened Thursday and lasted for hours, severely impacting services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. An outage affecting the nation’s air traffic control system Friday grounded all US flights for several hours and continued to disrupt air travel across the country over the weekend.
In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.
“This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” he said.
Monday's technical issues seemed to be centred at Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services.
A spokesman for US Bank said its systems were not directly impacted but that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed. Zelle is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.
A spokesman for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.
“An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,” the spokesman said.
Some Chase customers received a message that said, “Some services aren't available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.” (AP)
Edited by Cecil Wong

sources.news_title: Chicago-area Chase customers impacted by disruptions as bank works to resolve 'software bug' issue
sources.text:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- JPMorgan Chase said transactions are now processing normally after customers experienced disruptions to basic banking services due to a "software bug" that slowed or crippled transactions involving multiple banks, prompting some customers to seek cash and delay digital payments.
JPMorgan Chase said there is no evidence the issues were related to a cyber incident.
At Chase Tower in Chicago's Loop, business owner Lynn Kardasz went to withdraw cash after being unable to make payments through Zelle.
"I was at work, and I had a couple of colleagues that were trying to run some transactions, and they weren't going through, and with everything going on in the country and what happened with the Outlook and the FAA, I've decided to come here and withdraw some money," Kardasz said. "I don't know what is happening. I don't think any of us really do, and I guess I'm going to err on the side of caution."
The disruptions affected a range of banking services, including transactions with other banks. Some customers reported problems depositing checks or checking account balances. Others encountered issues with ATM withdrawals and online payments.
Another customer, Jocelyn Milhouse-Tanner, said she tested her account after hearing about the issues.
"I moved money from the savings to the checking just to make sure that it was functional, and I didn't have any problems, but when he tried to log on 10 minutes before, he couldn't get on," Milhouse-Tanner said referring to her relative.
Milhouse-Tanner also described taking precautionary measures amid the uncertainty.
"Going in to put some cash in and get some cash out, just in case," she said.
The outage comes just days after a rare nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop and a widespread Microsoft disruption that impacted email services for millions of people around the world.
While the exact cause of the Chase problems remains unclear, cybersecurity expert Andrew Hoog said consumers and businesses should expect more interruptions across industries as organizations work to strengthen their systems.
"As companies struggle to quickly patch to keep the AI-enabled attackers at bay, we're going to see more interruptions. I very much expect to see intermittent service availability issues, different types of problems," Hoog said. "This is an instrumental moment. We're going to look back at this time in five or 10 years and recognize that this is when things changed."
Hoog said companies are under pressure to update software more quickly to defend against AI-enabled cyberattacks.
"There's a high sensitivity right now in cyber security of if there is some vulnerabilities that need to be patched, we might need to patch that faster than we would normally do," he said.
Amid concerns about banking disruptions, the Federal Reserve said all Fed-operated financial systems are functioning normally.

sources.news_title: United Airlines, major US banks report system outages
sources.text:
Customers of major US banks reported difficulty accessing their accounts Monday, as United Airlines also reported a widespread system outage, elevating concerns about the durability of US digital infrastructure days after a tech failure grounded commercial flights nationwide.
United said later on Monday that it was able to quickly resolve the outage, which the airline clarified was not “a cybersecurity-related issue.” A JPMorgan Chase spokesperson told the Associated Press that its own problem resulted from a “temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system” and was “not cyber-related.”
The reports come as widespread integration of AI into digital architecture exposes new cyber vulnerabilities, and as experts and government agencies warn of adversarial governments and non-state actors seeking to exploit those vulnerabilities.
Asked about the disruptions Monday, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Anthropic’s Mythos announcement was “the inflection point at which it’s become apparent that all the bad software we’ve written for the last 50 years as humans is now going to be found out.”
“You’re going to see more of this, unfortunately, for the next few years,” Arora added. “I don’t think there’s a panacea… I think we’re just going to grind ourselves through it.”

sources.news_title: What to Know About the Banking Service Outages
sources.text:
Thousands of customers at multiple major U.S. banks are reporting difficulties accessing banking services on Monday after JPMorgan Chase announced a technical issue impacting its systems.
“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” the company, which has over 86 million customers across the U.S., wrote on X. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”
“We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today,” it added.
JPMorgan Chase did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for additional information regarding the issue.
Here’s what we know.
Which banks and services are being impacted?
Beyond Chase, customers at several other banks—including Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo, Capital One, and Truist—have reported problems on Monday, according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.com. Issues were also reported with digital money transfer service Zelle.
JPMorgan Chase noted that other banks where it was “party to a transaction” may also be impacted by the technical issue it is experiencing. But it added that “this is not a systemic issue.”
The company also said that its customers retained access to their accounts and money.
Zelle said in a statement to news outlets that its service is "operating as it should," but that "an issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers."
“Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds,” a spokesperson for the company said. “Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds. An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly.”
Zelle is owned and operated by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which is itself jointly owned by financial institutions including JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank, and Capital One.
A U.S. Bank spokesperson said to multiple outlets that “U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted,” but that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
How widespread are the outages?
Many Chase customers reportedly received a message on Monday that said “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”
By around 2 p.m. Eastern time, more than 4,700 customers at the bank had reported experiencing problems, according to Downdetector.com.
Reports of issues at other banks spiked around the same time, with just over 2,000 outage reports at Bank of America and 1,060 at U.S. Bank, per the site. Hundreds of customers at Wells Fargo, Capitol One, Truist, and Zelle also reported issues Monday afternoon.

sources.news_title: Major US banks face online outages, Chase rules out cyberattack
sources.text:
Days after Microsoft outage, top US banks see service disruptions due to 'bug'
Thousands of customers reported trouble accessing bank accounts, checking balances and transferring money on Monday. JPMorgan Chase traced the disruption to a software bug in its internal hardware systems, while other banks said transactions involving Chase could face delays.
Thousands of customers at some of the largest banks in the United States faced difficulties accessing their accounts and completing transactions on Monday, after a technical glitch at JPMorgan Chase triggered disruptions across financial services.
Bank of America, Chase, Wells Fargo, US Bank and Truist were among the financial institutions that attracted a spike in outage reports on Downdetector. Customers also reported problems with Zelle, the digital payments platform used by major US banks.
Chase, the largest US bank by assets, said the disruption was caused by a software bug in its on-premise hardware systems. The bank ruled out a cyberattack, saying there was no evidence that the incident was cyber-related.
"JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence it is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," a bank spokesperson said.
The bank added that customers could still access their accounts and funds, although some transactions were taking longer than usual to complete.
Downdetector recorded a sharp increase in complaints involving Chase, with thousands of customers reporting difficulties logging into their accounts, checking balances and completing money transfers.
The disruption also appeared to extend beyond online and mobile banking. Customers reported problems at some physical Chase branches, including difficulties making deposits, withdrawing cash and completing other banking transactions.
Fortune reported that Downdetector recorded nearly 4,500 reports involving Chase shortly after 1.30 pm Eastern Time, with the number crossing 20,000 by 2.22 pm.
Customers also reported problems with other financial institutions, although the scale of complaints was smaller than those involving Chase.
Wells Fargo posted a notice on its website acknowledging technical issues with online banking and advised customers to use its ATMs, branches and telephone banking services. Bank of America declined to comment on the disruption, according to Reuters.
The disruption also affected customers attempting to make payments through Zelle, a peer-to-peer digital payments network that allows users to transfer money directly between bank accounts.
However, Zelle clarified that its own network was functioning normally and that the problems originated at financial institutions.
"Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should," a spokesperson said, adding that technical issues at financial institutions could affect broader services, including payments made through the platform.
US Bank also clarified that its systems were not directly affected. However, customers attempting to send or receive Zelle payments involving another financial institution could experience delays.
Zelle is operated by Early Warning Services, which is owned by a consortium of major US banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank, PNC Bank, Truist and Capital One.
Chase subsequently said that the issue was not systemic and that other banks could experience transaction delays only when they were involved in transactions with the lender.
CHASE SAYS SERVICES RESTORED
Chase confirmed on Monday evening that transactions were processing normally again, after the bank worked to resolve the technical problem.
The incident comes days after a major Microsoft service disruption affected Outlook, Teams and Copilot. The outage, which began on Thursday, lasted for several hours and affected users across multiple countries.
The US aviation sector also faced disruption last week after a technical problem involving communications equipment at an air traffic control facility prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to temporarily halt departures nationwide.
While the sequence of disruptions has raised questions about the reliability of critical technology infrastructure, there is no established evidence linking the banking glitch to the Microsoft outage or the aviation disruption.

sources.news_title: JPMorgan Chase bank reports ‘software bug’ is disrupting transactions
sources.text:
JPMorgan Chase bank reports ‘software bug’ is disrupting transactions
Some customers reported on social media that they were unable to use their ATM cards or complete transactions
JPMORGAN Chase, the United States’ largest bank, reported trouble processing transactions on Monday (Nov 16), and said that the technical issues it was experiencing might have caused problems for customers of other banks.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems,” the bank said in a statement, adding that there was no evidence that the problem was “cyber-related.”
“It is taking longer than usual to service some customers,” the bank added. “This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.”
The banking issues were reported days after a global outage at Microsoft disrupted communications and work at schools, government agencies and offices around the world.
On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop after outdated air traffic communications equipment became overloaded and began to fail, officials said.
There was no indication that the disruptions had any common cause. But together, they added to a sense of gloom in social media chatter about troubles with modern technology.
“Our country has seen three very serious technology incidents over the past week,” Mike Chapple, a professor of information technology, analytics and operations at the University of Notre Dame, said in a statement.
“When we dig into the details, each one has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but they all point to a common theme: the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day.”
JPMorgan Chase, which serves more than 86 million customers at 5,000 Chase Bank branches across the United States, said its customers “still have access to their accounts and funds.”
“We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today,” it said.
Some Chase Bank customers reported on social media that they were unable to use their ATM cards or complete transactions at branches on Monday.
Customers at several other major banks, including Wells Fargo, US Bank and Bank of America, also reported problems on Monday, according to Downdetector.com, a website that tracks user reports of outages. Users also reported issues with the online payment platform Zelle.
US Bank said in a statement that its systems had not been “directly impacted.”
“However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” it said.
Zelle said it was “not down.”
“Zelle is operating as it should,” it said in a statement, which noted that customers who use the platform may be having trouble because of problems at their own banks. “An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” it said.
Wells Fargo and Bank of America did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The Microsoft outage, which started on Thursday and was resolved on Saturday, affected some of its most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot. Microsoft said the outage had been caused by a “technical issue” and not a cyberattack or AI agent.
The FAA ground stop, which was lifted hours after it was issued on Friday, created a cascade of flight delays and cancellations that continued over the weekend.
Government officials attributed the disarray to a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. Workers also noticed a second unspecified issue at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. NYTIMES

sources.news_title: Chase Banking Outage Follows FAA Ground Stop, Microsoft 365 Failure | WATCH | EURweb | Black News, Culture, Entertainment & More
sources.text:
*A nationwide Chase banking outage disrupted transactions Monday, November 16, becoming the latest major technology failure to expose vulnerabilities in systems Americans depend on daily.
Last Thursday, a Microsoft 365 outage interrupted email, workplace communications and other essential services. On Friday, a Federal Aviation Administration telecommunications failure forced a nationwide ground stop, disrupting thousands of flights.
Now, Chase customers are reporting problems completing banking transactions, accessing services and sending money through Zelle.
Three different systems. Three major disruptions in five days. And one increasingly uncomfortable question: How dependable is America’s essential technology infrastructure?
Meanwhile, about 1,500 customers reported issues with Bank of America on DownDetector as of 2pm Eastern, while hundreds of users reported outages impacting Zelle, Wells Fargo, and US Bank.
Chase Banking Outage Disrupts Transactions
According to NBC News and the Associated Press, JPMorgan Chase attributed Monday’s disruption to a software bug involving hardware systems operated on its premises.
The bank said the problem was not caused by a cyberattack and did not represent a broader banking system failure.
Although transactions were delayed, Chase maintained that customers still had access to their accounts and funds.
The problems affected online banking and some branch transactions, while customers also reported difficulties using Zelle.
Zelle said its payment network remained operational, explaining that problems at participating banks could delay transfers.
U.S. Bank acknowledged potential delays involving other financial institutions, while Bank of America and Citigroup said their own banking services were unaffected.
For customers awaiting paychecks, transferring money to relatives or making time-sensitive payments, even temporary disruptions can create immediate financial complications.
Chase said it was working to restore normal operations by Monday evening. A complete restoration had not been confirmed in the reports reviewed.
Microsoft 365 and FAA Failures Raise Broader Concerns
The banking disruption followed two other significant technology failures.
On Thursday, November 12, Microsoft experienced a worldwide outage affecting Outlook, Teams, Exchange Online and other Microsoft 365 services.
The disruption interfered with email and workplace communications, leaving users unable to access essential services.
According to BleepingComputer’s November 16 report, Microsoft traced the nearly 24-hour disruption to a previously undetected software bug introduced in July, increased network traffic and reduced server capacity.
Microsoft said services were fully restored Friday morning.
Later that day, November 13, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after instability in its telecommunications network affected aircraft communications and radar feeds.
According to the FAA’s November 15 explanation, excessive data traffic overwhelmed aging equipment, creating instability at 17 of the nation’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers.
The agency said approximately 3,500 aircraft landed safely during the disruption, with air traffic resuming Friday evening.
Investigators are examining whether equipment or installation problems contributed to the failure.
Are the Three Technology Failures Connected?
Despite their close timing, there is no established evidence connecting the Chase, Microsoft and FAA disruptions.
The organizations identified separate technical problems, and none has reported evidence that a cyberattack caused its incident.
Nevertheless, the failures illustrate how quickly technical problems can ripple into everyday life.
Workers lose access to communications. Travelers face cancellations and delays. Banking customers encounter uncertainty about payments and account transactions.
Customers affected by the Chase disruption should review account activity before retrying payments, monitor official bank updates and contact payment recipients if deadlines are approaching.
The larger question is whether the institutions Americans rely on have adequate safeguards, backup systems and modernization plans to prevent future technical failures from triggering widespread disruptions.

sources.news_title: Technical issue at one major bank causes disruptions for customers at banks in NC, across the US
sources.text:
DURHAM, N.C. (WTVD) -- Major U.S. banks experienced online and mobile service disruptions Monday, with thousands of users reporting issues involving Chase, according to customer reports tracked by Downdetector.com.
Bank of America, Chase, J.P. Morgan, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo and Zelle were among the services flagged by users. Thousands of the reports involved Chase.
Customers at a Chase branch in Durham said they encountered problems completing transactions.
"It's kind of weird. Everything's going at once," Chase customer Holly said.
Zuri Jimenez said she was unable to complete a transfer from her bank account to Apple Pay.
"I have been trying to transfer money from my bank to Apple Pay," Jimenez said. "There's an issue with it."
In a statement, Chase said: "Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete, but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible. This is a technical issue, not cyber-related."
The disruptions came days after a major Microsoft outage and aviation interruptions. All three incidents occurred within five days, though no connection has been established.
The series of disruptions has raised questions among some customers about the reliability of critical infrastructure.
"I am a little bit concerned," Jimenez said. "The airlines, it was really shocking, to be honest ... it surprised me, I've never seen anything like that."
Some Chase customers also reported being able to access cash through ATMs. It remains unclear when all services will be fully restored.

Amid the reports, U.S. Bank said that its systems are “not directly impacted” but that clients may experience transaction delays while trying to send or receive Zelle payments with another bank.
Zelle said in a statement that the digital payments network is not down and is “operating as it should,” but that “an issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers.”
More than 2,400 financial institutions use Zelle.
On its website previously, Wells Fargo said that there are “technical issues, but we’re working to resolve them as quickly as possible,” though it no longer states that on the page.
All financial systems operated by the Federal Reserve are currently operating normally, according to its website. That includes ACH transfers processed by the Federal Reserve between different banks.

sources.news_title: Chase blames a software bug for Monday’s US online banking outages
sources.text:
JPMorgan Chase blamed a software bug in its own on-premise hardware for Monday’s online banking problems at several big US banks. The bank said in a post on X that there was no evidence of a cyberattack. It aims to fix the issue by the end of the day.
JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence this is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.
Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue.
Customers still have access to their accounts and funds.
We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today.
— Chase (@Chase) November 16, 2026
Other banks felt it only where they were party to a transaction with Chase, the bank said, and “this is not a systemic issue.” Its customers still have access to their accounts and funds.
Thousands of reports
Reports about Chase on Downdetector peaked at nearly 5,000 around 2pm ET, Forbes reported. Customers of Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Zelle also logged problems, in smaller numbers.
Of the Chase reports, 52% concerned balances and transactions, 21% web log-ins and 17% transfers, The Hill found. Chase’s app told customers that some services were not available.
Some Chase customers said on social media they could not use ATM cards or finish transactions in branches. The New York Times reported those posts.
Other banks and Zelle
The problems centred on Chase customers and on people at other banks trying to transact with Chase, the Associated Press reported. Bank of America and Citigroup had no problems with their own services, according to the AP.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” U.S. Bank said in a statement.
Zelle, which a group of banks owns through Early Warning Services, said its network was working.
“An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” a Zelle spokesperson said.
The Federal Reserve’s own payment systems, including ACH transfers between banks, kept working normally. ABC News reported that from the Fed’s website.
A third outage in five days
The banking problems followed Microsoft’s Outlook outage, which began on Thursday. Microsoft called that a technical issue, unrelated to cyberattacks or AI agents.
On Friday, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after its air traffic communications network failed. Officials traced it to an Arkansas router upgrade. The FAA said it was not a cybersecurity incident either.
There was no indication the bank problems were related to Microsoft’s outage, The New York Times reported.

sources.text:
“I know now why you cry, but it’s something I can never do.” – The Terminator (T-800), Terminator 2
WTF?
Microsoft was down. America lost its air traffic control. Now, Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Capital One customers report outages. I’m no tech savant. But this seems problematic. This is how the New York Post described the latest systemic service interruption.
Customers at Chase, Bank of America, Capital One and Wells Fargo said they experienced outages Monday.
There were over 3,300 reports of outages at Chase and about 1,400 between BofA and Wells Fargo, according to Downdetector.com. Customers were unable to access their basic bank info like balances, the site reported.
Customers also began reporting outages at Capital One and the Zelle money transfer app.
Affected customers said online they couldn’t use their banking apps.
[UPDATE: United Airlines reported it was experiencing a systemwide outage.]
It makes me wonder, as a citizen with little knowledge of how safe America’s systems are in the AI age, whether the people supposed to run our electronic infrastructure know what they are doing. Even if it is ‘merely’ a tech failure and not the acts of hackers or enemies, our sense of security is taking a beating.
Additionally, if it isn’t hackers or foreign governments today, is America prepared and focused to deal with future electronic warfare attacks? Based on what I’m hearing from the current administration, my uninformed answer is “likely not.” Based on what? The rhetoric of this confederacy of dunces paints our national security threat as undocumented aliens. And the prospect of Iran developing deliverable nuclear weapons.
Really? The people who grow my food, butcher my meat, build my house, and clean my hotel room don’t seem like much of a threat to me. And I’m not losing sleep over the thought of an Iranian nuclear strike.
Defending against the wrong enemy
After 9/11, the Bush Jr. administration, along with the Republican big government national security types in Congress, passed the USA PATRIOT Act. It was a Big Brother-ish piece of legislation that enabled the federal government, in the name of national security, to expand its ability to spy on American citizens.
At the time, proponents argued that America’s advanced technology could keep the people safe from terrorism. How quaint.
Since then, tech has advanced exponentially. I imagine that we have a relatively good handle on the people who would blow things up. Certainly, nothing has come close to 9/11 since the original. However, this focus on bombers is antiquated. And the idea that immigrants, even those with evil intent, are a national threat is absurd.
Yet this administration added $170B to ICE’s budget to facilitate the removal of hard workers benefiting the economy, whose crime is that they are another country’s citizens.
If you are an American enemy, are you thinking the best way to bring the US to its knees is to blow up some buildings? Why go to that effort when you can let your fingers do the walking – or, in this case, the destruction?
It isn’t just ICE. Ukraine has shown that the best way to defeat, or at least stall, an enemy isn’t a gold-plated, big-weapon military bristling with tanks and jets. It is mass-produced cheap drones. Iran has further shown you can fight an enemy to a standstill without much of a military at all. However, those are defensive lessons.
On offense, Trump and his high-T sidekick, SecDef Pete Hegseth, are asking for another $500B on top of the almost $1T they already have to replace weapons that didn’t win a war in the first place. If there is a poster child for throwing good money after bad, this is it.
Money and the threat to safety
Meanwhile, in the era of Elon Musk and his fellow tech buccaneers, how do we know that the tech bros’ interests coincide with national priorities? Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick thought Nvidia selling chips to China was hunky-dory. Yet a rational thinker would have to wonder whether Lutnick’s family making money off the deals had something to do with it.
To add spice to that self-serving stew, Trump thinks the former Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, who resigned amid revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of having intelligence ties to Beijing, ought to get his job back. Trump also owns upwards of $62 million in Nvidia stock. And he is a man whose God is Mammon, and for whom “America First” means “Where’s my cut?”
AI and the road to perdition
Will AI be the Terminator’s Skynet made real? Is the human race teetering on the brink? Again, I have no idea. But my instinct is that it is not the proximate threat. The human race is outsourcing its decision-making to electronic actors. The rationale is efficiency and speed. But while it is now possible to create artificial intelligence, is there any plan to develop artificial common sense? Or an artificial conscience to shame a machine into behaving well?
Sadly, if AI reflects the people who created and promoted it, the answer is likely that the inherent behavioral controls most humans have will be absent in the new electronic brains. They will definitely never cry over their actions.
Bearing that in mind, it couldn’t hurt to look for a real-life John Connor.

sources.news_title: US banks face service outages as sectors suffer tech issues
sources.text:
US banks face service outages as sectors suffer tech issues
Major financial institutions in the United States reported service outages on Monday, as several sectors in America grapple with technical issues.
Customers at Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, U.S. Bank, Capital One, Truist, and Wells Fargo complained about difficulty accessing their accounts.
In a statement, a Chase spokesperson confirmed that some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete due to a technical issue, "but customers still have access to their accounts and funds."
A U.S. Bank spokesman said its systems are not directly impacted, but "clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays."
Though there is no evidence of a cyberattack at this time, the service disruption adds to growing concerns over major outages in the U.S.
Last Thursday, a major Microsoft outage lasted several hours and impacted services including Outlook, Teams, and AI assistant Copilot.
The next day, thousands of flights were cancelled following a nationwide ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration, FAA.
According to FlightAware, over 300 U.S. flights were cancelled as of Monday afternoon, down from about 2,300 on Sunday, 6,700 on Saturday, and more than 9,000 on Friday.

sources.news_title: The Bank Outage May Have Nothing to Do With Your Bank
sources.text:
If you were planning to do any banking today, good luck.
Customers of many major financial institutions experienced unspecified technical issues on Monday as thousands of reports flooded the uptime-tracking website Downdetector.com from people saying that they had issues using their banks in some way.
It is currently unclear which systems are having issues. However, the problem may stem from technical difficulties at JPMorganChase, the top retail bank, which holds over 10 percent of all US deposits.
“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems—there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” says JPMorganChase spokesperson Pablo Rodriguez. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”
Rodriguez adds that the bank is not experiencing a “systemic issue” but that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.” The spokesperson adds that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds” and that the bank is working to resolve the issues.
Apparent issues with the banks, credit unions, fintech apps, and credit card companies appear to begin around 9:30 am ET and peaked at around 2 pm ET. Many people also reported issues using Zelle, the peer-to-peer money-transfer system adopted by major banks. However, in a statement, Zelle denied its systems were the cause of the reported outages while acknowledging that issues at banks may impact people’s ability to use Zelle.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” a Zelle spokesperson says in a statement. “Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds.”
US Bank spokesperson Jeffrey Shelman also says the financial institution’s systems “are not directly impacted.” Shelman adds, however, that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
Seth Eisen, senior vice president of communications at MasterCard, says, “Our network is operating normally.” A Visa spokesperson says the company is aware of the payments issue, but that Visa’s systems are operating normally. A Capital One spokesperson similarly says the firm “has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time,” while a Bank of America spokesperson says its systems “have been operating normally today.”
According to reports on Downdetector, which is sourced to user reports rather than official statements and may not be accurate, the issues on Monday also impacted customers of Wells Fargo, TD Bank, Navy Credit Federal Union, and more. These companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Eisen, the Mastercard VP, says that DownDetector was “not correct” in the case of his company.
Whatever the cause, the timing of the issues may as well have been designed to get people looking for broader patterns. Last Thursday, Microsoft 365 experienced an unprecedented 24-hour outage that impacted millions of people, governments, businesses, and other institutions globally. Microsoft executive vice president Charles Lamanna said in a post on X on Monday that the outage, which impacted Outlook, Teams, and many other Microsoft cloud services, was related to an update that started rolling out in July but only began causing problems last week.
Soon after Microsoft resolved its outage on Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop order. This time, the issue was related to a problem with Air Traffic Control’s communications systems. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” the agency wrote in an FAQ explaining the outage. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”
The FAA’s five-hour ground stop resulted in thousands of canceled flights and otherwise disrupted travel for countless travelers. The impact of Monday’s banking outage remains unclear.

sources.news_title: Banking Closure Chaos Hits Americans Heading to Disney World
sources.text:
It's a warm afternoon at Magic Kingdom. The kids are tired, the line for a snack is finally moving, and you're ready to pay. Then you open your banking app to check your balance, and it won't let you log in.
For families who budget their Disney trips down to the last Dole Whip, that kind of moment can be stressful. A Walt Disney World vacation involves a lot of spending, and much of it happens through apps, linked cards, and digital wallets.
On Monday, a scenario like that suddenly felt a lot less hypothetical. Customers at several major U.S. banks reported trouble accessing their accounts and moving money, right in the middle of a normal weekday, and for some, possibly in the middle of a vacation.
Monday's Outage, at a Glance
- When: Monday, November 16.
- Who was affected: Customers reported problems with Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank. Downdetector also listed J.P. Morgan and Zelle as down or having issues, according to KTLA.
- What people reported: Trouble logging in, moving money, and cashing checks.
- How many reports: As of 1:50 p.m. ET, 24/7 Wall St. counted more than 4,600 Downdetector reports for Chase, more than 1,900 for Bank of America, more than 900 for U.S. Bank, and 800 for Wells Fargo. Forbes listed about 1,500 reports for Bank of America as of 2 p.m.
- A word of caution: Those numbers are user-submitted complaints, not an official count. None of the banks released their own figures.
- The Zelle angle: CNN reported that the issues at banks other than Chase appeared to stem from people sending money through Zelle to Chase accounts.
On the Record: What Each Bank Said
Chase, which saw by far the most complaints, said a technical issue was causing some transactions to take longer to complete. The bank stressed that customers still had access to their accounts and funds. Speaking to CBS News, a spokesperson made it clear this wasn't a security breach: “Chase Bank's services are experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue.”
Wells Fargo told customers its online banking platform was temporarily unavailable. “You can still access your accounts through our ATMs, banking locations, and customer service,” the bank said, according to 24/7 Wall St.
U.S. Bank said its systems weren't directly hit, but warned that Zelle payments sent to or from other banks might be delayed, according to CNN.
As of 2:16 p.m. ET, 24/7 Wall St. reported that Bank of America had not made a public statement.
The cause of the problems at Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank hadn't been confirmed, and there was no word on when everything would be fully back to normal. The disruptions came three days after a separate Microsoft outage on Friday, though no bank has tied the two together.
Following the Money at Walt Disney World
We haven't seen any reports of payment problems inside Walt Disney World linked to Monday's outage. But it helps to understand which Disney payment methods depend on your bank, and which ones don't.
Credit and debit cards: Accepted throughout the resort. These are directly tied to your bank, so a slowdown on the bank's end could, in theory, affect them.
MagicBand charging: Resort hotel guests can charge purchases to their MagicBands, but those charges are backed by a card on file.
Mobile Order: Food ordered in the My Disney Experience app is charged to the payment method linked in the app.
Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Samsung Pay: Accepted at most locations, though they still pull from your bank cards.
Disney gift cards: Once purchased, the balance lives on the gift card itself. You can also save gift cards to MyDisney Wallet in the app.
Cash: Accepted at most locations, though a few kiosks and carts only take electronic payments.
One more note: Zelle isn't a payment method inside the parks, but many groups use it to split costs between themselves.
Your Pre-Trip Money Checklist
You can't control a bank outage, but you can plan around one. Before your next Disney trip, run through this list.
- Bring a little cash. It's accepted at most spots around Walt Disney World, so it's a handy fallback.
- Grab a Disney gift card. It's a simple way to set aside vacation money. If you're already in the parks with cash, Guest Relations or a resort front desk can load it onto a gift card for you.
- Save that gift card in the app. Adding it to MyDisney Wallet in My Disney Experience makes it easy to use for Mobile Orders.
- Pack a backup card. Ideally, choose one from a different bank than your main card.
- Know your bank's backups. On Monday, Wells Fargo pointed customers to its ATMs, branches, and customer service when online banking went down.
- Settle up early. If your group splits costs, consider squaring up before the trip so you aren't relying on a transfer coming through mid-vacation.
Don't Let a Glitch Steal the Magic
A bank hiccup is frustrating on any day, but it hits differently when you're standing in the middle of a theme park. The good news is that a little planning goes a long way, and Walt Disney World offers enough payment options that you're rarely left without a backup.
We'll keep tracking the outage and share updates as the banks restore full service.
Now we'd love to hear from you. Were you in a Disney park on Monday, and did the bank issues affect your day at all? What's your go-to way to pay at Walt Disney World? Share your experience in the comments. Your tips might help another family avoid a stressful moment at the register.

Wells Fargo also acknowledged problems with its online banking services. According to NBC Chicago, the financial institution confirmed that it was investigating customer complaints and displayed a notice advising that online banking was temporarily unavailable.
U.S. Bank, meanwhile, said its systems were not directly affected, although customers attempting to send or receive money through Zelle involving another financial institution could experience transaction delays.
The incidents attracted national attention because consumers and businesses increasingly depend on digital financial services for everyday activities, including paying bills, monitoring deposits, transferring money, and managing operating expenses.
Although several major banks appeared in customer complaints, the available evidence does not show that each institution experienced a separate systemwide failure or that all reported problems stemmed from a common technical cause.
The disruptions were still being investigated in the Monday afternoon reporting reviewed for this article.
Thousands of Customers Report Banking Problems
Reports of banking difficulties increased Monday as customers turned to Downdetector to describe problems accessing accounts and completing transactions.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Downdetector had received more than 4,500 reports involving Chase by approximately 2 p.m. Eastern Time.
NBC Chicago separately reported more than 4,000 Chase-related complaints shortly after noon Central Time.
The figures represent customer-submitted reports recorded at particular times, not independently verified totals of affected banking customers.
Other institutions, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo and U.S. Bank, also appeared in customer complaints.
The Associated Press identified Truist among the financial institutions appearing in Monday’s reports.
Customers also reported difficulties involving Zelle, the electronic payment service used by many American banking customers.
Downdetector collects user reports to identify unusual increases in service complaints. Its information can provide an early indication of technical problems, but it does not independently establish the cause of an outage or the number of individual customers affected.
Multiple complaints may result from a single underlying issue, particularly when financial institutions and electronic payment services are interconnected.
For example, a customer trying to transfer money between two banks may encounter difficulties even if only one institution is experiencing a technical problem.
Consequently, seeing multiple banks on an outage-monitoring website does not automatically mean their internal systems failed simultaneously.
Nevertheless, the volume of complaints, combined with statements from Chase and Wells Fargo, confirmed that Monday’s banking difficulties extended beyond isolated customer experiences.
Chase Confirms Technical Problems
JPMorgan Chase, one of the largest financial institutions in the United States, acknowledged that an internal technical issue was affecting some transactions.
A bank spokesperson explained that certain transactions were taking longer than normal to complete.
Chase emphasized that customers retained access to their accounts and funds while employees worked to resolve the problem.
The bank also confirmed that it was addressing difficulties involving online banking.
According to NBC Chicago, Chase customer support acknowledged the issue in a response published through the social media platform X.
Some customers received notices saying certain services were temporarily unavailable.
The Associated Press reported that Chase characterized the problem as technical rather than cybersecurity-related.
This distinction matters because a banking technology interruption does not necessarily mean customer accounts have been compromised or deposits are missing.
Financial institutions run multiple systems that support account access, transaction processing, and other services.
A problem with one system can disrupt certain activities while other banking functions remain operational.
The precise technical cause of Chase’s disruption had not been publicly established in the afternoon reporting reviewed.
The bank did not provide a confirmed restoration deadline in those reports.
Wells Fargo Acknowledges Online Banking Interruption
Wells Fargo, another major financial institution, confirmed problems Monday.
NBC Chicago reported that Wells Fargo was investigating customer complaints involving online banking.
The bank posted a notice explaining that online banking was unavailable due to technical difficulties and that employees were working to resolve the problem.
This acknowledgment is significant because it distinguishes Wells Fargo from institutions identified only through customer-submitted complaints.
A confirmed online banking interruption does not necessarily mean that every banking service is unavailable.
Financial institutions typically maintain separate systems for branch operations, ATMs, payment processing and online account access.
Depending on the nature of a technical problem, customers may still be able to conduct certain transactions through alternative channels.
Customers experiencing difficulties should contact their financial institution directly to determine which services remain available.
The reviewed reporting did not establish a definitive restoration time for Wells Fargo’s online banking services.
Bank of America and Truist Appear in Customer Reports
Bank of America and Truist were among the other financial institutions identified in Monday’s customer complaints.
However, the available information requires an important distinction between confirmed institutional problems and customer-submitted reports.
Chase acknowledged a technical issue involving transactions and online banking.
Wells Fargo confirmed that it was investigating online banking difficulties.
U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly affected.
Bank of America appeared in Downdetector reports, but NBC Chicago reported that the institution declined to comment when contacted about the situation.
The reviewed reporting did not establish that Bank of America and Truist each experienced separate, confirmed institution-wide outages.
Customers may encounter difficulties using financial services for reasons that do not originate within their own bank.
Electronic payments often involve multiple institutions, service providers, and processing systems.
A problem affecting one part of that infrastructure can produce complaints involving several organizations.
This interconnected structure helps explain why reports involving different banks may increase during the same period without proving that every institution experienced the same technical failure.
Zelle Payment Delays Create Additional Concerns
Zelle was another service appearing in customer reports Monday.
The electronic payment network lets customers of participating financial institutions send and receive money through their existing banking apps.
Zelle is operated by Early Warning Services, a financial technology company owned by several major U.S. financial institutions.
Its owners include Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.
Because Zelle facilitates payments between accounts at different banks, transactions can depend on systems operated by multiple institutions.
U.S. Bank specifically addressed that issue Monday.
The financial institution said its own systems were not directly affected but warned that customers sending or receiving Zelle payments involving another bank could experience delays.
NBC Chicago also reported that Zelle directed attention to the problem involving Chase rather than confirming a separate networkwide outage.
This distinction is important.
A delayed Zelle transaction does not necessarily indicate that the entire payment network is unavailable.
A payment may be delayed because of difficulties involving the sending institution, receiving institution, or another part of the transaction process.
The available reporting did not establish that Zelle experienced a nationwide systemwide shutdown.
Nevertheless, the complaints illustrate how problems at one financial institution can inconvenience customers conducting transactions with another.
Consumers should verify the status of pending payments before attempting to send the same amount again.
Why Banking Problems Matter to Consumers
Online banking has become an essential component of everyday financial management.
Millions of Americans use mobile applications and banking websites to monitor deposits, check balances, pay bills and transfer money.
For many households, digital banking has largely replaced routine visits to physical banking locations.
The convenience of these services has created expectations that financial information and payment systems will remain accessible throughout the day.
When digital services become unavailable, or transactions are delayed, consumers may experience uncertainty about their financial obligations.
A customer attempting to pay rent, confirm a paycheck deposit, or transfer money to a family member may be unable to complete the activity as expected.
Even temporary interruptions can create complications as payment deadlines approach.
Customers may also have difficulty determining whether an electronic transaction was successfully submitted.
For example, someone trying to pay a utility bill may receive an error message without knowing whether the payment remains pending.
Submitting another payment without confirming the original transaction could result in duplicate charges if both payments eventually process.
Consumers should therefore review transaction histories and contact their financial institutions when necessary before repeating electronic payments.
It is also important to distinguish temporary banking service problems from account security concerns.
An unsuccessful login attempt does not automatically indicate that an account has been compromised.
However, report unfamiliar transactions or unauthorized account changes immediately.
Small Businesses Depend on Reliable Banking Access
Banking technology interruptions can also create operational challenges for businesses.
Small companies depend on electronic financial services to manage cash flow, receive customer payments, compensate employees, and pay suppliers.
Many businesses use multiple financial platforms to conduct daily operations.
A company may receive payments through one provider, process payroll through another and use a banking application to transfer operating funds.
When digital banking services become temporarily unavailable, those activities can become more complicated.
A contractor may need to confirm a customer deposit before purchasing materials.
A retailer may need to transfer money to pay a supplier.
A restaurant operator may need to verify that sufficient funds are available to cover payroll or inventory purchases.
These examples illustrate potential consequences of banking technology interruptions.
They do not establish that Monday’s disruptions caused widespread payroll failures, merchant-processing shutdowns, or measurable nationwide business losses.
The reviewed reporting did not establish a verified estimate of economic losses attributable to the November 16 banking problems.
Nevertheless, the incident demonstrates why businesses should maintain accurate transaction records and understand which alternative payment methods are available.
Restaurants Face Particular Financial Challenges
Restaurants are among the businesses that depend heavily on reliable financial technology.
An independent restaurant may process numerous transactions each day through credit cards, debit cards, online ordering systems and electronic payment services.
Restaurant operators also rely on banking services to pay food distributors, manage payroll, and monitor operating expenses.
Because restaurants frequently operate with tightly scheduled financial obligations, uncertainty surrounding deposits or transfers can complicate cash flow management.
However, it is important to distinguish online banking access from merchant payment processing.
A problem accessing a bank’s mobile application does not automatically mean that a restaurant’s credit card terminals have stopped functioning.
Similarly, difficulties involving Zelle do not establish that debit card networks, credit card processing systems or restaurant point-of-sale equipment are unavailable.
These services may operate through separate infrastructure.
Restaurant operators should determine which services are affected before changing payment procedures or advising customers that particular transactions cannot be completed.
Maintaining financial records, communicating with vendors, and establishing alternative authorized payment arrangements can help reduce the consequences of temporary disruptions.
For independent restaurants already managing rising operating costs and unpredictable customer traffic, dependable access to financial information remains an important part of daily operations.
Was the Banking Disruption a Cyberattack?
The appearance of several major financial institutions in outage reports naturally raised cybersecurity questions.
However, the available evidence did not establish that Monday’s banking problems resulted from a coordinated cyberattack.
Chase specifically described its problem as technical rather than cybersecurity-related.
That statement applies to the issue Chase acknowledged and should not be interpreted as a completed investigation of every complaint involving other financial institutions.
Technical disruptions can result from software errors, infrastructure failures, communications problems, transaction-processing difficulties, or complications involving third-party technology providers.
Determining whether separate incidents share a common cause requires technical evidence.
The fact that customers reported difficulties involving multiple banks during the same period does not, by itself, prove that the institutions experienced the same underlying failure.
The reviewed reporting also contained no verified evidence that Monday’s problems reflected bank insolvency, missing customer deposits, or a broader financial crisis.
The confirmed concerns involved access to digital services and transaction processing.
For consumers, that distinction matters.
A temporary inability to access online banking does not necessarily mean that money held in an account is unavailable or at risk.
Customers Should Remain Alert to Banking Scams
Banking disruptions can create opportunities for scammers attempting to exploit customer uncertainty.
Fraudsters may send messages claiming that an account has been suspended or that customers must immediately verify their identities to restore access.
These communications may arrive through email, text messages, telephone calls, or social media.
Some may contain links to fraudulent websites designed to collect passwords, security codes, or other sensitive financial information.
Consumers should avoid providing confidential account credentials in response to unsolicited communications.
Anyone seeking assistance during a banking disruption should contact the financial institution through its official website, established mobile application, or verified customer service number.
Customers should also be cautious about social media posts claiming that banking systems have been compromised without credible supporting evidence.
A legitimate service interruption does not justify sharing sensitive financial information with an unfamiliar individual.
If suspicious transactions appear, customers should contact their banks immediately.
What Customers Should Do During Banking Problems
Consumers experiencing online banking difficulties can take several practical precautions.
First, check official communications from the financial institution to see whether the institution has acknowledged a service problem.
Second, avoid repeatedly submitting electronic payments without confirming whether earlier attempts remain pending.
Third, retain transaction confirmation numbers, payment records, and error messages whenever possible.
Fourth, contact the bank directly if you cannot complete an urgent transaction through the normal digital channel.
Fifth, review account activity after services return to normal to confirm that delayed transactions were processed correctly.
Customers facing payment deadlines may also wish to contact the intended recipient and explain that a banking technology problem is affecting their ability to complete a transaction.
Available alternatives will depend on the financial institution, account type and specific service involved.
Consumers should not assume that every banking function is unavailable simply because a mobile application or website is experiencing difficulties.
ATMs, physical branches, telephone banking and other services may remain available, depending on the institution and the nature of the disruption.
When Will Banking Services Return to Normal?
The reporting reviewed Monday afternoon did not establish a definitive restoration schedule covering every institution identified in customer complaints.
Chase indicated that it was working to resolve its technical problem.
Wells Fargo confirmed that it was investigating online banking difficulties.
U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly affected but acknowledged possible delays involving Zelle transactions with other financial institutions.
For other banks appearing in customer-submitted reports, the available information did not establish a uniform explanation or restoration timeline.
Customers should consult their individual financial institutions for current service information.
Although Downdetector can indicate whether complaint volumes are increasing or decreasing, those numbers do not constitute official confirmation that a problem has been fully resolved.
Restoring one service also does not necessarily mean every reported transaction delay has been cleared.
Banking Reliability Remains Essential
The November 16 banking disruptions highlight the importance of dependable financial technology in an economy increasingly driven by electronic transactions.
Consumers rely on digital banking to manage household finances, monitor deposits and pay everyday expenses.
Businesses depend on financial technology to maintain cash flow, compensate employees, and meet financial obligations.
When those systems experience difficulties, even temporary interruptions can create uncertainty.
Monday’s events do not establish a nationwide banking crisis or a coordinated attack against the American financial system.
The verified developments include technical difficulties acknowledged by Chase and Wells Fargo, potential Zelle transaction delays identified by U.S. Bank, and customer-submitted complaints involving several other prominent financial institutions.
The precise causes of every reported problem and the final restoration status were not established in the afternoon reporting reviewed for this article.
As banking services continue evolving, maintaining reliable digital infrastructure and communicating clearly with customers will remain essential responsibilities for financial institutions.
For now, consumers and businesses experiencing difficulties should monitor their accounts, verify pending transactions, and rely on official information from their banks.
